newsitem.title: UK: Weak straight-run fuel may compress price spreads.
newsitem.headline: Weak straight-run fuel may compress price spreads.

text.p: The European market for low sulphur straight-run fuel oil is teetering on the edge of a fall, with 250,000 tonnes of unwanted product on offer, traders said on Thursday.
Some expect a dip of about $5 a tonne towards $120, which threatens to compress the price range across the various fuel grades on both sides of the Atlantic.
Demand from the United States has dried up in recent days after a two-week buying spree which may have delayed a fall.
Low sulphur straight-run is the most expensive fuel oil and is used by refiners to upgrade into higher value products such as gasoline.
It typically commands a premium of some $20 a tonne over the poorest quality, high sulphur grades which are burnt in power stations or used to fuel ships.
"There are about eight sellers with nearly 350,000 tonnes between now and the middle of October. I see perhaps 100,000 tonnes of demand," said one trader.
Its value has already fallen sharply against crude since last spring: from an average 80 cents discount to Brent in 1995, it now stands at a $3.00 per barrel discount.
Structural changes to European refining have contributed to the lower values against Brent this year, as have recent outages at plants in the U.K.
North European refiners tend to buy flexible, short-haul, sweet North Sea crudes because they enable late changes to timing and quantity as well as a wide selection of grades.
But the thirst for sweet crude ensures a steady stream of low sulphur straight-run fuel from refiners in Germany, Belgium, Ireland and the U.K., resulting in occassional mini-gluts.
Currently, straight-run fuel enjoys a $7 a tonne premium over low sulphur cracked fuel used in power stations.
Some dealers expect that differential to narrow further, looking back to last winter when it averaged just over $6.50.
But it is beginning to look cheap compared to high sulphur cracked fuel, the cheapest fuel grade which may now provide a floor.
Over the past year it averaged nearly $23 a tonne above high sulphur fuel, but now stands just $13 over. --Sam Arnold-Forster, London newsroom, +44 171 542 4984
